title: Dynamic Programming: Fibonacci with Memoization
oneLiner: Same recursive fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) as before -- but check a cache before recursing, and the exponential blowup disappears.
keyTakeaway: Memoization turns Recursion: Fibonacci's O(2^n) into O(n): every fib(k) gets computed at most ONCE, cached, and every later call that needs it again returns instantly instead of re-expanding the whole subtree underneath it. The exact same recursive structure, but every value computed exactly once -- that's the entire idea behind top-down Dynamic Programming.
explanation:
Recursion: Fibonacci's recursive definition is correct but wasteful -- fib(4) gets computed from scratch by BOTH fib(6)'s call to fib(5) (which needs fib(4)) AND fib(6)'s direct call to fib(4), completely independently, with zero memory that the other branch already solved it. Memoization fixes this with one addition: before doing any real recursion, check whether this exact input has already been computed and cached -- if so, return the cached value immediately; if not, compute it the normal recursive way, then cache the result before returning. This is called TOP-DOWN dynamic programming: the recursive structure stays exactly the same as the naive version, "top" (the original call) recursing "down" toward the base cases, just with a cache remembering everything along the way.

Step through the visualization and compare it directly against Recursion: Fibonacci's for the same-shaped problem: every fib(k) that would have been recomputed from scratch instead shows up as a "[cached]" frame that returns INSTANTLY, with no further recursion underneath it -- fib(1), fib(2), fib(3), and fib(4) each get computed exactly once here despite being needed multiple times across the call tree. For a small n like this the difference in step COUNT looks modest, but the shape is what matters: naive Fibonacci's call count roughly DOUBLES with every increase in n (true exponential growth), while memoized Fibonacci computes each value from 0 to n exactly once -- linear, not exponential. At n = 30, naive Fibonacci makes over a million recursive calls; memoized Fibonacci computes only 31 distinct values (about 59 calls, because every fib(k) above fib(1) still calls both children; the repeat calls return straight from the cache).

The same idea generalizes far beyond Fibonacci: ANY recursive problem where the same sub-problem gets solved multiple times independently ("overlapping subproblems") is a memoization candidate -- caching turns repeated expensive recomputation into "compute once, look up everything else." See Dynamic Programming: Climbing Stairs (Bottom-Up) for the same underlying recurrence solved the other direction, without recursion at all.

fib(4) already in the memo -- return 3 instantly, no recursion.

complexity.note: Each distinct fib(k) is computed once and cached, collapsing the exponential call tree to n distinct calls; the memo and the recursion depth are both O(n).
